utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I assume that there are no procedural matters to be raised and that, after I have invited the witness to make a solemn declaration, that you could start the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as I also do understand, major portions of the testimony to be received through Rule 89(F)?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's our application. I will deal with that as soon as the witness has been sworn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Bjelica, I assume. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher will help you to adjust so that the earphones will not drop off. Mr. Bjelica, good morning in this courtroom. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The next is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Bjelica. You'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your name is Milovan Bjelica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness be given a copy of the exhibit bundle, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness turn to tab 19, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist the witness so that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In tab 19, Mr. Bjelica, we find a document which is headed "Milovan Bjelica Rule 89(F) evidence." It's right that you had a chance --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- to look at this document and confirm its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I handed to the registrar this morning the signed copy, B/C/S only, which the witness signed and dated yesterday. I hope that that complies with the formalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it that there are no -- oh, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Obviously we would appreciate also having a copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether usually all pages are signed off, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if there's no problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean, the -- my learned friend can look at the original. The witness simply signed and dated, otherwise it's absolutely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if we could have that opportunity at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Often on each page there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's not the procedure we adopted. If the Court feels that should be done, it needs to be done now before we begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness looks at it -- Mr. Josse, of course you present the evidence that's also -- if you say this is what the witness was given, this is what he read, this is what he signed on the last page, then there's no specific need to ask the witness now to sign every page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the very helpful advice that the Defence received from Mr. Zahar, we have prepared a summary of this evidence to be read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have a number of copies of that summary. Again, I'm unclear as to whether the Chamber would like a copy in front of them as I read it or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily, because the main purpose of it is to inform the public that what is approximately the content of the evidence which is led but which is not in full audible to the public. So it serves mainly the public character of the trial rather than that it serves the Chamber, who receives of course the original statement. Please read it but slow enough to -- for the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to do that. Could I just address the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you provided a copy to the interpreters, because that would certainly be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't, I'm afraid, but we've got three here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber could do without. So, Madam Usher, could you please distribute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, while the interpreters receive this document, what I'm about to do is read a summary of the document that you have signed. It's a few pages long. It's in English only but of course it's going to be translated into your language as I read it.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour would indicate when I can begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the interpreters have received it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And through the smoked glass I see the sign, so please start, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the period after the first multi-party election in 1990, the witness was chairman of the SDS municipal council deputies' club in Sokolac. In May 1991 he was elected vice-president of the Sokolac municipal committee of the SDS. In September 1991, he was nominated Sokolac representative in the SAO Romanija Assembly, which convened for the first and last time that same month. At the end of 1991, the witness was elected director of public enterprise "Romanijapetrol." On 13 January 1992 he was elected as president of the SDS municipal committee, replacing Mirko Malovic. Based on an agreement between SDS and SDA, it was decided that Serbs and Muslims would share power at the municipal level in Sokolac. The agreement, insofar as it concerned the division of posts in the police system, was confirmed by the then-leadership of the BiH MUP at a meeting in Sarajevo, which the witness attended as chairman of the personnel commission of Sokolac municipality. On 30th of March, 1992, the Ministry of the Interior was set up and Zoran Cvijetic was elected as SAO Romanija MUP minister. After a period of time, autonomous region interior ministries were renamed security centres. Thus Zoran Cvijetic became head of Serbian Sarajevo security centre. At the end of 1991/beginning of 1992, a reserve police force, the Territorial Defence, and the reserve staff of the 216th Mountain Brigade of the JNA were present in Sokolac. Mixed patrols of army and police personnel regularly made rounds of Serbian and Muslim communities and provided security for camps with refugees from Croatia. Neither then nor later was any paramilitary group formed in Sokolac, nor any other armed group of any sort. Before the outbreak of the war, Muslim municipal deputies and all other Muslim municipal officials left their posts following instructions from the SDA leadership in Sarajevo. They set up their own parallel municipal structures in Kaljina and Knezina. One such structure was the police force. On one occasion a postal vehicle was stopped by Muslim police in Kaljina, the mail was thrown into the river, the vehicle looted, and a police escort detained. When efforts were made to investigate this incident, the Muslim police would not cooperate. Despite the departure of SDA deputies from the Sokolac Municipal Assembly, it continued to function and serve the citizens of Sokolac throughout the war. There was a Crisis Staff at the municipal level, which included members of SDS, SDP, industrial managers, representatives of humanitarian and health organisations, and non-party persons. There were no combat activities in the territory of the municipality of Sokolac when the first armed clashes occurred in Bosnia. However, subversive and terrorist activities were conducted by members of the Muslim paramilitary unit the Patriotic League, which was formed in the territory of Sokolac long before the war started, somewhere in autumn of 1991. The Patriotic League had been arming itself since then and forming combat units since December 1991. According to some people, Patriotic League members were hiding arms in Muslim religious buildings, the very same buildings in which these weapons were distributed. The number of wounded and killed members of the army and the police tasked with the maintenance of security in the Sokolac region was increasing. In summer 1992, the VRS brigade command issued a request that those people who had not been mobilised in the army or police to hand over illegal weapons and explosives. No one acted upon this request. The subversive and terrorist attacks still occurred, especially in the territory of Sahbegovici, Kaljina, and Knezina, which resulted in killing and wounding of many civilians. As a result of these events, the VRS command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade decided to undertake a demilitarisation of the region in order to guarantee security to the civilian population as well as to its own soldiers. During the demilitarisation of the Sokolac municipality armed clashes occurred in the following villages: Meljine, Sasevci, Iseric Brdo, Zulj, Sahbegovici, Pedisama, Rakitinci, Novoseoci, Kutima, Kalimanic, and Micivoda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I see the transcribing is a little bit behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have every sympathy. They're not the easiest proper names for an English speaker. Throughout 1993 and 1994, subversive terrorist Muslim actions resulted in the death and injury of many civilians. Houses were looted and set on fire. During the war, there were no prisons or camps in Sokolac. Persons suspected of taking part in or organising subversive terrorist acts, whether Serb or Muslim, were put into custody in military security offices in Cavarinama and Knezini and questioned. All Muslim terrorist activities were conducted according to the directive issued on 14 April 1992 by the BiH Territorial Defence commander Colonel Hasan Efendic. When war broke out, there were no medical institutions in Sokolac or Romanija, everything was in Sarajevo. Muslim subversive terrorist groups destroyed equipment used for transmitting electrical energy in Visegrad and Rogatica, as a result of which the whole Romanija region was left without electricity and water. Main roads from Serbia were cut off and were subjected to continuous attacks from Srebrenica and Bratunac. Paramilitary ambushes took place, which resulted in the deaths of many Serbian civilians. Traffic was also blocked in Konjevic Polje, as a result of which food and other supplies could not get through. During the 1992-1995 war, 288 members of the VRS and MUP from the Sokolac municipality lost their lives, one-third of which were killed in terrorist actions and ambushes carried out by Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, perhaps just for the information of the Chamber, having looked at the 65 ter summary, now the 89(F), the evidence led gives quite some details about, I would say, violence committed by Muslims. Do we have to understand that as in terms of -- I see three major options. We'd like to know which of them we should pay specific attention to. One could be that it's important for - if it ever comes to that - sentencing, just to give a balanced view of what happened. Second possibility is that it would undermine the evidence or contradict the evidence we received through Prosecution witnesses. For example, I see some of the villages mentioned also appear in some of the evidence we received during the Prosecution case. And the third option I perceive is that there would be something like self-defence situation, or -- which of the three we should specifically focus on when hearing this evidence. Could you give us some guidance in that respect. If you have a fourth or a fifth option, fine, but I took the most obvious ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Really, I perceived the second option I'm bound to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second option, okay. That's -- not excluding the others ones, I take it, but that's the focus of -- that's the real -- the importance of this evidence. I would say the primary importance of this evidence. Okay. Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, in the first paragraph of your 89(F) evidence, you deal in part with your political history. I would like to go into that in a little bit more detail now, if I may. It is right that you graduated from Novi Sad in Serbia -- what is now Serbia --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in economics?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You worked in an accounting department of a state enterprise called Romanija in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You then became the director of Romanijapetrol, another state enterprise, a job you held up until 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From 1994 to 1997, you were commercial manager of another government enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From 1998 to the year 2000, you were secretary-general of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes -- or it was the director of the directorate of the Serbian Democratic Party. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From the year 2000 to 2003, you were president of the municipal association of Serb Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It wasn't a municipal association. It was the Assembly of the city of Serbian Sarajevo, made up of six municipalities, and they are: Sokolac, Pale, Rogatica -- It was called Serbian New Sarajevo, Serbian Ilidza, Serbian Old City, and another one. Those were the municipalities that made it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were removed from that job by the then-High Representative of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, I was removed on the 7th of March, 2003. The explanation was that I financially supported a person who was accused of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What's the name of that person, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this may be a subject we'll return to later, but was the allegation that the High Representative made against you a true one?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Nothing was ever proved, and I claim again before this Trial Chamber that I never supported in any way, financially or otherwise, to Karadzic or anybody else, nor did anybody ask for me to extend such support. On two occasions I was brought in by NATO and SFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina in May 2004, and I spent 30 days in an unknown location. And the second time I was taken in was between the 31st of August and 27 September of the same year, that is 2004. During the investigation -- and I can't complain of the way the investigation was carried out, it was done very correctly by those who interviewed me, and the duration of the whole investigation was 60 days or so. Whatever I had to say, whatever I knew, I told them. Up to year 1999 nobody even looked for Dr. Karadzic. He negotiated at the time with many people from the international community. And let me just say this: All this time while I was a -- being held at that location, reports were sent by NATO and SFOR command about Milovan Bjelica being at a safe place, about Milovan Bjelica cooperating, and that they were happy with the conversations that they were holding with Bjelica. They ended their conversations, they handed me over to the public security service of East Sarajevo. They said: We are done here, we have nothing whatsoever to do with Bjelica, what we needed to do with -- managed to accomplish. This was the official report of the NATO commander on the 14th of June and then on the 27th of June [as interpreted] when I was released for the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. You were asked whether the allegations were true or not. I do understand from your answer already from the first three or four lines that they were not. Then you started to give a long explanation. I saw, Mr. Josse, that you were about to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just give the guidance that I think there was ever reason to intervene at that moment. If you have done it a bit more strongly, you would have been successful, I take it. I also do understand that the witness just came in. Mr. Bjelica, please focus very much on the question. Just to give you an example, if someone would ask you whether you came by plane to the Netherlands, you could say: Yes or no. Or you say: No, I didn't come by plane, I came by car. But we don't need to know what company, we don't need to know what food was served on board. These are all details. If we're interested to know these details, we'll ask you. So first answer the question briefly, and then Mr. Josse will let you know what further details he will need. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Bjelica, I'll add one other thing: I think in my original question I said it may be a subject we'll return to later but I was simply at this stage trying to deal with your history. Because after you were removed by Lord Ashdown, it is correct, isn't it, that you have been unemployed ever since?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'll come in a moment to your present predicament, but before I do that, the political jobs that I've asked you about hitherto were jobs that you were paid for. They were full-time bits of work. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what we now need to do is go back in time, please, and look at some of your other political activity before you were employed in politics, so to speak. It's right that you were a member of the League of Communists, but you left when the SDS was formed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, I left the League of Communists when I joined the SDS. I never actually sent a notification in writing to the League of Communists informing them that I actually left them, which was also the case with all the other people who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were elected to the Sokolac Municipal Assembly in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were a member of the Crisis Staff in Sokolac --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in 1992? You were elected a member of the Executive Committee of the SDS in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Locally, as we have heard in the 89(F) summary, you became president of the SDS municipal committee in -- at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 13th of January, 1992, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, I want to turn briefly to your present situation. You are presently incarcerated in Bosnia, facing an allegation of fraud, the allegation relating to matters after the war had ended. Is that right in an absolute nutshell?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I have been charged with abuse of official position. Allegedly I signed a loan agreement, and that loan, the funds were used for the electoral campaign of the SDS in 1998. And allegedly those funds were never returned by the SDS. And the SDS never returned the loan because the then-leadership --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. You've told the Chamber what the essence of the allegation is. I want to ask you one other thing about it. It's right that there are a number of people who were charged with you, one of whom this Chamber has heard evidence from, namely Momcilo Mandic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, Momcilo Mandic is the one who was charged with that crime first. He was one of the owners of the bank that granted the loan which was allegedly given to the SDS, but there are other charges against him. In my case, there's just one count of the indictment against me, which is the loan that was used to finance the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you have pleaded not guilty to that count and you are awaiting trial. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, some of these --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- documents have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, Mr. Josse, I think tab 19, the 80 -- no, the 89 -- yes. The statement, not the summary, but the written statement signed by Mr. Bjelica on the 5th of April, I think it was --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, some of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Some of the documents in this bundle have been translated; others, unfortunately, have not yet been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turning to tab 16, Mr. Bjelica, a document that isn't translated. It's right that you took the trouble to obtain this certificate which states that you are a man who has no criminal convictions, certainly as of the 7th of February, 2005?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. This was issued on the 7th of February, 2005. I tried to apply for certain jobs, but I couldn't find a job so I obtained a certificate proving that I had never been convicted and that I had never been tried. And this certificate was issued with a purpose of finding a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who issued the certificate? Who is the issuing authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just for my information, is there any dispute about whether Mr. Bjelica -- perhaps it serves other purposes but is there any dispute about whether Mr. Bjelica was ever prosecuted or convicted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I don't know what we're heading for, but if that's the issue, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is simply it, but clearly when the Defence bring a man to a court in custody, and the Chamber is aware that he is in custody, it seems unusually important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- on this occasion to try and bolster his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you could have just discussed it with Mr. Margetts. A jury might be under an impression that someone who is in custody might be a criminal, whereas this Chamber is aware that whatever prosecutions are taken against a person, that one sits the first time. So we had no reason, as a matter of fact, to even think about it, where a jury might think that. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In those circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has not got a number yet. It has been copied already, so -- the problem is it should be translated. We do understand that this is an unusual --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it has been sent for translation. If it hasn't, I won't exhibit it; if it has -- it has been sent, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could still be withdrawn. It serves no purpose than that the witness, uncontested, says this is the first time that he's involved in any criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm content to withdraw the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- I may at this juncture indicate that there have been certain public pronouncements by authorities relating to Mr. Bjelica's conduct, and it could be that as a result of that this document may become relevant. But the question of actual trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not aware of that and whatever -- I mean, the document, I take it, is just reflecting to what extent a criminal record exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever people say in public, whatever they think about Mr. Bjelica -- as long as you are not going to lead any evidence that people say he was charged before, he was convicted before, I think it's not very relevant. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The power-sharing agreement in your municipality, how did it work? Was it effective?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Based on the inter-party agreement among the three ethnically based parties, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, positions were distributed at the republican level, at the town level, and at the municipality level across Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Sokolac municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. The reason I'm going to stop you, Mr. Bjelica, is you have the advantage in one sense of having had a significant amount of your evidence produced in this written form. So the Chamber are aware of what you're saying because they have read the document that you are looking at at this precise moment. My question was a very specific one, was: How effective was the power-sharing agreement in your municipality? That's where you worked, where you lived, where you were active in politics.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: An agreement was reached and everybody was happy, both the Serbs and the Muslims. There were no Croats in the municipality. The agreement was implemented to the full.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did it start to break down?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The agreement started breaking down at the moment when the Serbs did not accept the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina - I suppose you are going to ask me about that later - and the Muslims asked the municipality to organise this referendum. The Sokolac municipality did not want to organise the referendum on independence because it was not supported by the Serbs, and then it was done in an undemocratic and unlegal way. The consensus was not respected. We would not stand by the referendum. And in the meantime, the Serb assemblymen signed a document, the 20 of them, organised into the committee on protection of national interests and equality of nationalities and national minorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was not accepted, and then a new organisation was set up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this spilled over to all the municipalities. And those people, the Muslims, were not satisfied with the fact that the Serb assemblymen did not want to organise a referendum. Then they said that they would organise their power, their municipality, and that they would organise their own referendum. That's how the referendum was organised. Only the Muslims participated in the referendum unhindered, nobody prevented them from voicing their opinion, and there were no -- there were no incidents during the referendum. They were given official premises in the SDA and in the office of the president of the SDA, Pecacina [phoen], and the vice-president, Hajrudin Smajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, when you refer to Serb assemblymen, it would be Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the municipality Assembly, there were assemblymen of both Serb and Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were Serb assemblymen in the municipality, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the Croatians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not -- reading the last line, it's still not perfectly clear. When you're talking about the Serb assemblymen signed a document, the 20 of them, were you referring to 20 Serb members of the Municipal Assembly or were you referring to 20 members of any other assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20 assemblymen in the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 20 Serb assemblymen who were seeking protection of their national interests through the committee on the protection of equality of people's national minorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they'd wanted to prevent a violation of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia. And all this was taking place in the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the Croatian war and what effect that had on municipal relations.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: When the war in Croatia started, we knew that a number of Muslims volunteered to fight in Croatia in -- as members of illegal formations. Those units were called HOS units, MUP units, ZNG units, whatnot. And the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina wanted to preserve Yugoslavia as it was and to preserve the JNA. We publicly supported the JNA, and we invited all those who were in favour of Yugoslavia to respond to the call of the only legitimate military institution and force in the former Yugoslavia, which was the JNA, and to respect the orders of superior commands. And this is what was done. In Sokolac also we issued an invitation to our men to respond to the call of the JNA rather to organise themselves or to support any paramilitary organisations. In Sokolac there were a few companies of the then-216th Brigade based in Han Pijesak and they went to Croatia to fight in the war there on the order of the -- their superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is right that you have in your possession a recording in part of a funeral in December of 1991 of a serviceman killed in that war?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that one of the witnesses - and I read it somewhere or I followed it in the media, and it was also said by SDA representatives from Sokolac - that volunteers were sent from Sokolac municipality to Croatia to fight in the war there in 1991, that they got killed there, and that we received them, their bodies, as heroes. We buried them under some fascist symbols, Chetnik symbols, whatnot. And I claim before this Trial Chamber that only one young soldier, who was a conscript at the time, a conscript in the JNA, Aleksandar Jolovic was his name, he got killed somewhere near Osijek. And maybe two or three months, the Croatian armed forces, the ZNG or MUP, would not allow the JNA to exchange the bodily remains. Once the exchange was carried out -- and I have the recording because the late Aleksandar Jolovic's father gave this to me, it features the funeral that took place towards the end of 1991, and you can see the symbols of the former JNA, the army of the former Yugoslavia, which was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what we're going to do is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before we play that, may I ask one clarifying question. In your previous answer you said you invited - I think you said - your men to respond to the call-ups of the JNA. And then you said: "... rather, to organise themselves or to support any paramilitary organisations." What made you invite them -- invite them to join paramilitary organisations rather than the regular army? Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hadn't read that transcript in that manner. Maybe clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then it's unclear to me. I just read what it says on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was some concern from one of -- from Mr. Sladojevic about that as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then let's first try to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm bound to say I was concentrating on something else. It needs clarification, and I would be grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you issued an invitation to your men to respond, and then could you please -- there might be a translation problem. Could you please repeat that portion of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter believes that she said "rather than," and the word "rather" has not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Municipal Assembly of Sokolac municipality, and I myself as a deputy, we had the majority, we invited the citizens of Sokolac to respond to the Yugoslav -- join the Yugoslav People's Army, not paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been clarified now, and it's good, I think, because it could give a totally false impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I'm grateful, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevant CD is quite long. We intend to fast-forward it. There is no sound and I'm simply going to ask the witness in due course to identify the various speakers at the graveside, two in particular of some importance, and to recollect what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were at this funeral, weren't you, Mr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation of that answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I helped organise the funeral. We were all included in organising the funeral because it was the first victim, he was a young soldier, and the municipality took it upon itself to help the family with the funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're going to start playing it and I'll give instructions for it to be fast-forwarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we could fast-forward to the gravesite, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very important, if I might be allowed to comment. It is important to see that you have the five-pointed star as the insignia. No other insignia is anywhere. The official insignia of the Yugoslav People's Army, which was the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Feel free to comment at any time. That's exactly why we're playing it, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, fine. You can see here officers of the Yugoslav People's Army; Colonel Krsmanovic, and Colonel Vehbija Karic, who was later on a high-ranking officer of the BH army and member of the Patriotic League. Have a look: On the helmets you can see the five-pointed star and all the uniforms are uniforms of the JNA. Nothing else, no other insignia. And the flag with a five-pointed star is covering the coffin. The only other insignia we see here is the cross because he was a believer, an Orthodox. And this is the decoration that his family was posthumously handed by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Vehbija Karic, colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, and handed that decoration over to the man's -- the young man's father. So he was killed and he was buried with insignia of the Yugoslav People's Army and not, as we heard allegations of, Chetnik insignia or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we're just going to fast-forward to Colonel Karic, if we may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There you can see it again, the five-pointed star. Take a look, please. On the coffin, the flag with the five-pointed star, the tricolour flag. The Serbs supported in Sokolac the Yugoslav People's Army and all the legal institutions of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was legal and nothing to do with those working illegally who are trying to turn events around and prove that with this funeral. You can see the five-pointed star, the flag, the Yugoslav flag, and all the rest, the uniforms, et cetera. Once again, the president of the municipality, Mr. Tupajic, delivering a eulogy on behalf of the socio-political organisations of Sokolac, saying that he hoped nothing like that would happen again, that he died in defence of Yugoslavia. And this was confirmed by the other speakers who took the floor, as well as the uncle and a lawyer from Belgrade of Aleksandar Jolovic says that he laid down his life for the third Yugoslavia, because Slovenia had already left. He's the man with the hat. He's the son of a national hero, Jolovic, from World War II. And the last speaker was the priest, Orthodox priest, as is customary. And then Mr. Vehbija Karic, who referred to him as a hero of the new Yugoslavia and who had laid down his life, he said, for Yugoslavia, his country, and the defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who's speaking -- we just saw the second speaker there. Who's that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: That's Professor Milorad Savic. His speech was delivered on behalf of the young people and pupils of Sokolac municipality because the soldier was a young man and a member of the youth organisation of Sokolac, so that was on behalf of the professors from secondary school, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did we see Colonel Karic in the video?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, he was in front of the municipality building, and you'll see him again delivering his speech. You can show that footing of him delivering his speech. And he said that the Serbs had no aversion towards officers of other ethnic groups and that a Muslim who was a high-ranking officer at that time came to speak at a meeting of this kind and nobody had anything against it because we felt that he was supporting the Yugoslav People's Army as well and that he was going to fight for the preservation of Yugoslavia. There you had Mr. Karic a moment ago. The cemetery is next to the church, a religious facility, religious site. And another important point is this: There was just one victim in Croatia from the Sokolac municipality. Here you see it. That is Aleksa Krsmanovic, a colonel, and next to him -- that's the uncle that I was talking about who's a lawyer and who mentions Yugoslavia and the preservation of Yugoslavia in his speech and that all efforts should be invested to that end and that his forebears in 1914 and 1941 to 1945 laid down their lives to protect Yugoslavia and that they had national heroes among their family members holding decorations, and so on. That was a speech delivered on behalf of the family. But nobody mentioned any Greater Serbia or greater Serb nationalism or anything of that kind. Here you can see it again, the decoration -- the insignia of the Yugoslav People's Army, the decoration of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Presidency decision to accord it. This is the honour platoon, honorary platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who's that? Stop there. Who's that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: That is Colonel Vehbija Karic, a colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, and later on he was a high-ranking officer in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether the Patriotic League as well or not, I don't know. That was to the end of 1991. So that the colonel, who was a Muslim, delivered a speech at this funeral, not as many wished to portray it as being something else with different insignia and so on. So to the last moment, very last moment, we tried to do everything in our power to give our contribution as far as was possible to preserve Yugoslavia and to preserve the Yugoslav People's Army, which was a multi-ethnic army, which is evidenced from all this footage that we have been able to see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does that need a number, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it needs a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could you guide us as -- because it seems that this evidence contradicts allegations of a Chetnik-type funeral and demonstrates that it was not of such a kind. Do you remember exactly, because it might have slipped out of my mind, where we heard this evidence that this was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't have those particular notes with me. I may have them, in fact, in the Defence room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, could you assist us on where we find the evidence so that we know what is contradicted? Or was no evidence led?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no specific memory at this stage of evidence regarding this funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But there were other gatherings in the region at that time where evidence was led --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not this specific funeral?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I can't say we led evidence on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you please check, because if there's evidence, it makes a lot of sense to show us the picture that contradicts that impression. If, however, there is no evidence and as the witness said it was at that time said in the press that Chetnik matters -- I mean, that's not part of the evidence. I don't hope that the Defence is going to lead evidence just not to contradict the Prosecution's evidence but to contradict what was published at that time in the press. Because I take it for granted that the press was not impartial. So therefore, the whole exercise is very important if it contradicts evidence, and the Chamber hopes and prays that the Defence does not understand its task to be to contradict whatever was published at that time in the press, because then we would need another ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for that guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In relation to this Exhibit D161, the witness has given evidence as to the content of the speeches. We have the visual of the funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It would be useful if we could obtain the audio as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but I take it that no audio is available, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an audio-recording. I have the tape in my room with the audio part, the audio-recording. So there's no problem. I can provide it. You can see it, that was Vehbija Karic, and it is our aim to prove that the Muslims attended the funeral and that it was a multi-ethnic event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, there is nothing which you have to prove here. The only purpose for you being here is to answer the questions in accordance with the truth. No burden of proof whatever upon you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I could help to this extent as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- I know, because I had some limited personal involvement in this, that the witness provided a tape, a videotape, of what the Court has just seen, to the Defence. It is not possible to play videotapes in this courtroom, so we've been told. I -- if that sounded critical, it certainly wasn't meant to be at all. And as usual, the technicians were very helpful some time in advance, and they -- of their own volition, or at least at our request, transferred the videotape onto a CD --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And lost the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and the sound was not on the CD, as we understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could -- I do understand that these are kind of technical problems, but nevertheless it would be good to have the text of at least the speeches, because there seem to be real speeches on -- available. Perhaps, Mr. Bjelica, if you could provide that tape to the Victims and Witnesses Section, and the section will then, I take it, give it to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and help there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean, that's clearly difficult for them. He probably needs to provide it to one of the prison officers, realistically. The Victims and Witnesses Services have very little to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we need very specific instructions for the prison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- it will it be copied, I take it, so that the original will be returned to you, but could you -- Mr. Registrar, I invite you to take the necessary measures that the Detention Unit will be informed about you handing over a tape so that we can listen to the words as well and not only see the pictures. This, Mr. Josse -- still, the relevance is very much dependent on what evidence we receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make two very quick observations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We should still have a videotape somewhere. Neither of the two gentlemen who are assisting me today were involved in the operation of transposing the video onto a CD. My second observation is this: The Defence do not intend to provide a transcript of this funeral. Frankly, Your Honour, it's exactly the same as the Tuzla convoy point; we don't have the resources to do that. And so we will make the tape available to the Prosecution. What Mr. Margetts requests is not unreasonable. The burden will be on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that since the witness has now testified about the contents of the speeches that at least the audio gives an opportunity to you, Mr. Margetts, to check, on the basis of the audiotape, whether there is any reason to dispute the testimony of the witness in this respect. So you first could listen to it, perhaps, with the assistance of a language assistant and, if need be, then to transcribe it and have it translated and have that added to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just in terms that my learned friend will understand, what we're seeking here is the best evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can't argue with that. I emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then, Mr. Margetts, you will receive either the tape or a copy of that tape; and you can do with it as you deem fit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about whether your municipality received any refugees from the Croatian war.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: During the war in Croatia, there was an exodus of Serbs and people of mixed marriages. So there were women who were Croats, children from Papuk, Zvecevo and Podravska Slatina. Several hundred families arrived on the territory of Sokolac and a certain number in the Pale area and elsewhere, and we put them up in Sokolac. And some families were put up in the hotel in Sokolac, other families would take in families coming into the village and give them support and assistance for the time they spent there. So that was one of the special tasks, care and attention to the displaced persons and refugees coming in from the war-engulfed areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next would like to ask you about your knowledge of Muslims in your municipality beginning to arm before the war.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: In the Serbian Democratic Party through our personnel in the Ministry of the Interior, Territorial Defence, and Defence Ministry, as well as in the state security, and in certain talks held with the population in the Sokolac municipality - and that was the similar case in other municipalities - we learnt that the Muslims were preparing themselves for war, that they were arming themselves, rallying in mosques, in certain houses, in certain locations, and so on and so forth, and that they were wholly bent on propagating the declaration once written by Alija Izetbegovic which was published in certain Sarajevo dailies at that time, which instilled more fear amongst the Serb population throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only where we were. And we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there because it's right that if we look at paragraph 13 of your 89(F) evidence, you set out various matters.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, this is just -- this just confirms what I said a moment ago; all the information that we had, that it was all correct. And the police, when controlling traffic, would stop vehicles and make checks. And on one occasion there was a religious official who was found with a Kalashnikov on him. I think it was produced -- manufactured in the 1980s or the 1990s. I know that that was made public. There was a lot of ammunition. And he said in the Sokolac municipality, where he was stopped under Mount Romanija, he was prosecuted, that man, and then there was a deputy for Gorazde, Hadza Efendic. He was found with a bomb and other weapons in his car while he was driving towards Sarajevo, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you mention in paragraph 13 an article in Oslobodjenje dated the 24th of September, 1992. Do you have that article?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think that I was going to talk about this, but on the 24th of September, 1992, in the Sarajevo daily Oslobodjenje - and you can see it on the Patriotic League's site and you can get it from Oslobodjenje newspaper as well - that Mevludin Smajic gave a statement, and he was in the staff of the command of the Patriotic League, he made a statement to the effect that in 1991 -- throughout 1991, he worked to organise the Muslim people on the territory of Sokolac municipality, that he went to Croatia and brought in weapons, and that every other day he would go to Vitez and bring in explosives, and at one point he had brought in 120 kilogrammes of explosives. And in January 1992, he had on his list 866 members of the Patriotic League who were well-trained and we knew that they were undergoing training, that training had been organised for them, sabotage work in Kumrovec, and that certain groups went to Libya as well. We had information to that effect before the war, and that he had -- 40 per cent of these members were well-organised members of the Patriotic League, well-trained. And this was also borne out by Mr. Isic, who was the deputy minister of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, I asked you a very straightforward question. I expected the answer to be: No, I don't have the article, and then I was going to ask you why and to explore that sort of thing. You must try and answer the question that I am asking you. Is that clear? I know you've got a lot that you want to say to this Chamber, and they understand as well, but you must try and answer the questions that I ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to note at this juncture that what we have here is not only the presentation of a press article, we in fact have much less. We have someone giving evidence as to their memory of the press article, and I just would like to note that and ask, through the Chamber, whether Mr. Josse considers that he wishes to lead that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what that means, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be -- Mr. Margetts, I think Mr. Josse started exploring whether the press article exists. If it doesn't exist, then still, having read something in a press article is not, as such, irrelevant nor, as such, unreliable, nor, as such, incredible. So therefore, at the same time, Mr. Josse, I'm more concerned about the content of all of it to have a lot of details. And I'm also concerned about what would have been the sources of the press article. We have heard now, I think from both sides, approximately a hundred times that reporting was usually very partial -- nevertheless, we accepted some of it, as mainly on events rather than on the interpretation of events. So it's not without concern that I allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm moving away from the press article. Could we look at tab 20, please. Your Honour, I make no criticism of this, quite the opposite, but this was a document that the Defence received very recently by way of Rule 68 disclosure, and so it has not been translated nor, I suspect, sent for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it if the Prosecution was able to identify it as Article 68, then -- no, one second, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That the Prosecution is aware of the approximate content. Please proceed, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could just say that this was published in Oslobodjenje, which was published in the federation in Sarajevo, not in the Oslobodjenje published by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bjelica, your attention is now drawn to tab 20, and Mr. Josse will put questions to you in that respect. Could we perhaps, for "omot spisa," Mr. Josse, what would that approximately be, so we have an introduction to the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I -- you received a copy of this yesterday, quite late, to be fair to you, Mr. Bjelica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you had a chance --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- to look through these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. I knew of such things. There were many such cases that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, again, the question was: Did you have an opportunity to look at the documents? I take it since you start commenting on it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Very well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The learned Judge --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're going to take this slowly and in stages, Mr. Bjelica, because we do not have a translation and that makes certainly my life and most other English speakers in this courtroom life very difficult. Looking at the very first page, we see that it says "o-m-o-t s-p-i-s-a." You're not on the first page, Mr. Bjelica. The very first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cover page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do those two -- perhaps you could read out "omot spisa," or perhaps I could ask the interpreter to tell us what they mean, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the interpreters tell us what "omot spisa" means.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "File cover," "cover page."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That doesn't help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, I rather think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a complete file, as one can make out, isn't it, relating to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in fact we're going to see this type of thing on various other occasions during the course of your evidence. What we have here are all the documents relating to the Prosecution of this man, Mr. Halilovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Chamber has some assistance. If one looks at the index --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, perhaps first, there could be easily a misunderstanding here. It is Alilovic instead of Halilovic, and since the name Halilovic, of course, is only too well-known, I draw the attention to this small imprecision in the transcript, page 37, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. So, Your Honour, if one goes to the index at the front of the bundle --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not you, Mr. Bjelica, it's not going to help you but it will help the learned Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There we see a summary prepared by the Defence of these various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In essence, Mr. Bjelica, what was Mr. Alilovic alleged to have done?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Mr. Alilovic was charged with possession of automatic weapons of foreign make, Kalashnikov, that is, and that he possessed a large quantity of ammunition which was illegal. I believe that this was in January, I don't know exactly when. In any case, it was in 1991, and this is one of the proofs to show how Muslims armed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you go to three pages from the end of tab 20, a document that is numbered 01398231 and is dated the 15th of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: In -- my number under the date the 15th of February -- no, no, no, you're right. You're talking about the Prosecution number. I have that document, I have that page in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, this shows that in fact the proceedings, in the end, were stopped in some way. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, because of the statute of limitations under the criminal code. The summons could not be delivered. In the meantime, the war took place, the -- and according to the statute of limitations which was in effect by then the judge had to close the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I'm going -- first of all, I'm not going to ask you whether this would be a suitable time to stop, but usually my breaks are filled with other meetings so I would like to have a break now. Could you at the same time during this break perhaps identify a few lines which are of direct relevance for the understanding because the only word, you'll understand, is "sudija," which I do understand. But all the remainder and then it's not yet entirely clear as far as ethnicities are concerned or what ethnicity was the accused, or at least the suspect. It seems to be a Republika Srpska decision, at least that's what I take from the top. Could you try to identify those portions that, in the absence of a translation, at least gives us a better way of understanding some of the literal wordings of this document. Mr. Bjelica, we'll have a break. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I first of all deal with the issue of the videotape, and I've been asked by the registrar, who's very -- who's worked very hard on this subject during the break, to do this in public. We have found the videotape --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's no need anymore to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have handed it over to our learned friends. There is no need -- we have checked that the sound works on it. Apparently it could have been played in court, we were unaware of that and I apologise if in any way I suggested the opposite, and there is no need, as far as I can see, for the UNDU to be asked to provide the copy that the witness has in his possession there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I leave it to you whether you, in addition to the testimony of the witness about the content of the speeches, whether you would like the speeches then to be played rather than the whole of the video again. And moving through a video goes slower than moving through a DVD. Mr. Margetts, same for you. If you find it relevant in -- in addition to what the witness told us, to let us hear the content of the speeches, we'll hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Back to tab 20, please. The third page of tab 20, the document that is dated -- I don't know if it's altogether clear, it seems to be August of 1992, but it bears the number 1992 at the top, third page -- no, not that one. Go to the first page of tab 20, please, Mr. Bjelica. The first page. One --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What we see here is in the middle of the page where it says: "dana 13/1/1992" it sets out the allegation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Just a moment. I can't find it. 13 January -- yes, yes. This is a witness statement -- actually, this is the statement of the accused, based on his statement. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Try and answer my questions, please, Mr. Bjelica. What I would like you to do, please, is slowly read out that one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'd prefer larger portions to be read by one of your team members. They are more use to speed of speech, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Mr. Mujanovic to do it, Your Honour, because he has been helping me with this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mujanovic. So we start with "Stoje" and then "Dana."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "13 January 1992, in Sarajevo in the immediate vicinity of the town hall from an unknown person, in an authorised manner he purchased an automatic rifle, Kalashnikov, factory number S4BJ4751, calibre 7.62 millimetre, and four rounds of ammunition and 101 pieces of bullets for the aforementioned rifle, calibre 7.62 millimetre. The aforementioned weapon and ammunition were found on the accused in an Argentina 2000 car -- Argenta, I apologise -- in Podravanje during a regular check-up by an employee of the public security station Sokolac. In other words, in an authorised -- in an unauthorised manner he purchased fire weapon and ammunition by which he committed a crime of unlawful possession of weapons or explosives pursuant to Article 213, paragraph 1, of the penal code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And for completeness, and I'm not going to ask this to be read out, if you turn, Mr. Bjelica, another one, two, three, four pages, there we have the statement of the accused, Mr. Alilovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It is correct that weapons were found on him, that he -- that he admitted, this is all correct, but I don't think he paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, I know - and I'm sure the learned Judges know - you are trying your best, but listen very carefully to the questions that I am asking you. I wasn't asking you at that particular point in time to comment on the evidence; I was simply asking you to verify one or two things. You must understand that we have a serious handicap - not your fault at all - namely, we do not have these documents in English and that makes life rather difficult. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question is simply this: The document that you are now looking at is the statement of the accused man, Mr. Alilovic, where he explains how he came by these fire-arms. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to help the Chamber as to the ethnicity of Mr. Alilovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Mr. Alilovic is a Muslim and purportedly he obtained the fire-arms in Sarajevo. And we only want to make a contribution to the Muslims arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, Mr. Josse asked you very friendly to focus on the question. The question was whether -- what the ethnicity of Mr. Alilovic was. Of course he's asking that in order to demonstrate to the Chamber that at least this Muslim obtained a weapon, or at least was suspected of it. There's nothing -- you don't have to bother about to make a contribution to anything but the truth. And the questions are focussing, I think, as a matter of fact, on the same matter as you have in mind at this moment, which is quite understandable, but just leave it to Mr. Josse. Answer his questions. He'll ask for further details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, I even asked for the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Defence. He was a Muslim. I apologise. It won't repeat again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page that we're looking at, we see two other names. Could you first of all read out the title in capital letters above the name of Mr. Predrag.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: "A statement taken by ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What ethnicity is Cajic Predrag, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Predrag Cajic is a Serb. At the time he was a crime inspector in the public security station of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same question in relation to Mr. Borovcanin, Ljubisa Borovcanin. What is the title in block letters above his name, please? Read that out.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: "Present."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what ethnicity is Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Serb, an employee of the public security station. He was either the deputy commander or the head of the crime police. I don't know exactly what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, only answer this if you can. If we turn on another three pages, we see the document that we looked at before which deals with the discontinuation of the proceedings, you have told us, because of the statute of limitations. We see that that document is headed up "Republika Srpska." Are you able to explain how it is that Republika Srpska became involved in these proceedings which started before that republic had been founded? Only answer if you know, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The date is 15 February 1996. This was after the Dayton Accords were signed, and the basic court in Sokolac was part of the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska and the only court in -- courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina were in Republika Srpska. And the basic court in Sokolac took over all the cases which were not resolved by them. And an order came from the Ministry of Justice for them to finish the cases, and that's why the basic court in Sokolac finished this particular case in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've no further questions, Your Honour, about these documents. I don't know whether they've been given a number. If they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet, from what I understand. I take it that the whole bundle gets one number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, we were looking at paragraph 13 of your 89(F). Could you turn back to tab 19 and go to paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see there the name a few lines up from the bottom of paragraph 13 Atif Saronjic and Konda Karmen.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Atif Saronjic. Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see that you have said that they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken in. I don't know what -- yes, arrested, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was your understanding as to why they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The police probably had information about Mr. Atif Saronjic, who was a highly ranking officer of the JNA, he was a corvette captain of the JNA. He left the JNA in 1990 and got involved in the organisation of the Patriotic League of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The intelligence service and the police knew that he was in charge of operative work on the ground and that he was accompanied by Konda Karmen who had documents, but nobody knows whether this was a true personality, whether this was a true identity, which proved to be the case during an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You see my hand. The reason I had my hand out was you need to slow down a little bit. As I said to you already, I appreciate it's not easy, but apart from answering the questions, when you answer the questions, you need to answer them in a slow pace because obviously the interpreters have to try and keep up with what you're saying. Do you understand, Mr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I do understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we turn now to the last document of tab 13, which again, sadly, has not of yet been translated since some time ago, Your Honour, I think. Now, let me try and summarise this document. This is a document that was sent by Velibor Ostojic to the Red Cross in, it appears, the 30th of April, 2000 -- I beg your pardon, 1992. And it states that the MUP of the RS had custody of the following individuals on your list, so presumably it must have been a list that the Red Cross had provided to the government of the Republika Srpska. Is that your understanding of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see that numbers 11 and 12 are the two people whom you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, but under number 4 you also have that person. So the people that were looking for that person didn't know what number they would appear under, and they looked under Karan Saronjic, so you can analyse that. You see, number 4 is the same person, whereas the person was taken into custody under the name of Karmen Konda.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Read out, please, the whole entry, including the words in the two sets of brackets under number 4, just those two lines. Read them out slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: "Karan, not known, possibly it is a case of Karmen Konda and not Saronjic, as was listed in the list under number 12." That means that they were looking for another name, Karan Saronjic, whereas down here we have Karmen Konda who was arrested, and it says here that possibly it was a case of Karmen Konda and not Saronjic, as was stated, so it's the same person. That means there was something suspicious, and they were never able to ascertain the identity of the person in question. And I asked in the police station about that person, and later on it turned out that they were very important people in the patriotic -- in the organisation of the Patriotic League and the activities of the Patriotic League in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know where in Sokolac these people were detained?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: In the police station. They were in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For how long were they in detention?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The police determined that. We just learnt later who these people were and that they worked in intelligence and visited certain persons, and they gave statements to that effect to the police, and the police sent it on to the Office for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, those particular statements and everything about them that they deemed necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And have you any idea when they were released from detention in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, straight after the request made by the government of Republika Srpska, and the names were handed in to the International Red Cross Committee and the International Committee -- they were handed over to the International Red Cross Committee, so that was straight away, straight afterwards, a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether their detention was by way of any legal process; that is, their detention in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do think that they have the whole dossier, the whole police file, on this case as well as for the others who were taken into custody. I can't really know this because it's up to the organs of the interior to deal with. But everything was done according to the legal process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you able to assist as to who in the municipality would have been responsible for liaising with the Republika Srpska government to organise the transfer of these people and that type of thing?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, that could have been done by the Ministry of the Interior.
