The president of the Municipal Assembly would have to have been informed, and he would contact the government in that regard. And the Sokolac municipality had its own commission, just like any other municipality, its commission for searching for and exchanging persons who were missing and prisoners of war, and the president was Mr. Dragan Podinic. And this was constitutional procedure according to the rules and regulations that were in force at the time. So they cooperated closely with similar commissions from other areas, a different entity as it is today, and with the ICRC, the International Red Cross Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that document have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your -- questions I'm going to ask you, Mr. Bjelica, are by their nature rather disparate, so we're going to go to a completely different topic now but still in the pre-war period, and I want to ask you to have a look at this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is the Variant A and B document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you're aware now of the existence of that document. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I heard it mentioned at trials here, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And indeed, you have dealt with the matter in correspondence to this Tribunal. Could we turn to tab 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: When the trials in Hague started, I got to know this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, Mr. Bjelica. Could you turn -- or could the usher help you turn to tab 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is D9, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it's written on the top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this document has an introductory letter from Mr. Blewitt, who was then deputy Prosecutor in the Office of the Prosecution, and thereafter there is your reply to his inquiry. We see the reply there. It's been dealt with in this court previously. Does that set out what you understood in November of 2001 to be the position so far as the Variant A and B document is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, yes. I wrote this and I sent it. It went through the Ministry of Justice. I understand the situation fully. I've understood it, and they asked whether we still have these documents in the archive. And I don't know what you want, whether to comment on what I wrote here. I'm not quite clear on your question. What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, in particular, the very last paragraph, please. There are two sentences. As far as the first sentence is concerned --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that still the position as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, that's it 100 per cent. This question was never posed, nor was it solved, nor were any similar documents compiled, and that's the situation today as well. That's how I understand it now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the second sentence where you told the Ministry of Justice that you were given information that a certain number of retired officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army were responsible for the document? Where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, all of us together in the party tried to see where this information was coming from regarding these documents, and I asked on one occasion - I think he was General Subotic, the defence minister in the government of Republika Srpska, the first defence minister - whether he had any knowledge of these documents and whether they had anything like that in the Ministry of Defence, because we had to give a response. And he said no. And I said I was the president of the party and never heard of them. And then he said that a certain number of individuals, retired persons, that they had the same information, as did some other people, that they were in the divided municipalities, that is to say whether you had Serbs and Muslims, a mixed population of Serbs and Muslims, and that the Muslims and the Croats already had such Crisis Staffs. They had Crisis Staffs and they, for a certain number of individuals and municipalities, they wanted to copy that, and that's why they compiled these documents. And a group of retired officers -- well, that was the situation, if this is true, this Variant A and B. Now, as far as Sokolac municipality is concerned and the Romanija area as a whole, as far as I know, a document of this kind never reached us, never arrived anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could we ask the witness: When you were -- when you were told that these were retired officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army, did you ask for any names or were any names mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, because it wasn't a party matter. I don't know who -- well, it wasn't linked to the Serbian Democratic Party, what they were asking at the time -- asking for at the time. We weren't asked to investigate. I said that I asked around, asked people whether they knew about this. Perhaps I shouldn't have even done that, even asked around, because it didn't exist, it wasn't in the archives, but I wanted to help, to throw light on the situation, to resolve the issue because it was an issue since these trials in The Hague began. I think that someone did it with the right intentions. It might have been slipped in or whatever, I don't know, apart from the official SDS organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you: Did you learn whether this was a -- kind of a secret action by those military men or by those officers or -- did you learn anything more apart from that it was just a group of retired JNA soldiers -- officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I didn't do anything special. I know that there were officers like that in our area. For example, retired officers, that is. They would come in and then they offered their services and we would send them to the commands; what they did with them, I don't know. But quite certainly, they did it on their own bat. I don't know that they did anything else. Perhaps it was well-intentioned, perhaps not. People who were ready to accept their support and assistance, they were old officers, bureaucrats, and so on, who could not find their way in the newly arisen situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber received evidence that at later stages reference was made to such a document in a very official setting. I think it was Assembly meetings, but could you explain why such a document of what you say, well, just the initiative of some JNA -- retired JNA officers, whatever they had in mind, took such importance at a later stage at Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. What I'm saying is that I never have seen this document, never saw it until recently. And I have no information that Badza [phoen] was in an Assembly anywhere. Possibly, but I never saw it. He never came where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you turn to tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, though it doesn't say it, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 4, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in the index is P835.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 4, please. You have had a chance to look at this intercept of a conversation between you and Radovan Karadzic on the 27th of December of 1991. Firstly, do you have any recollection, 15 and a half years later, of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, I remember that there were some conversations, but this has reminded me, jogged my memory, and I think this is quite correct. I have no objections to make. Had I not read it, I wouldn't have known what we talked about, but when I saw this, then quite certainly it is correct, a correct rendition.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Reference is made at the start of the intercept to invoices being put through someone called Krajisnik. To whom is that a reference?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, these weren't sent on, but I'm not quite sure whether they were Slavo Krajisnik or Mirko Krajisnik. I'm not quite sure now because we had some telephone conversations with the two of them; we never saw them. But I don't think anything came of this. It was never realised. This business was never realised. They were two systems full of fuel that had to be paid for. We weren't able to meet those requirements, so this was a business transaction that never went through. And President Karadzic called us up at that time because we had contacted as an enterprise and as a municipality the competent institutions and asked for their assistance to prevail upon the Ina and Energopetrol companies to provide resources for the vital institutions of the municipality; that is, to provide us with fuel, with petrol. But they didn't do so. They didn't cater to the Romanija area. When these two cisterns turned up, this transport company appeared and they asked the president or whoever, Tintor or whoever, whether they needed fuel anymore, he said ask for Sekovic. So we needed petrol but we couldn't comply with the price, we didn't like the price because it was supposed to be 45 dinars first of all, that was the figure quoted, and now the next price was 58 that was being asked for, 58 dinars, and we didn't have the money to pay for that and so this never materialised. This business transaction never went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, under tab 4 we find, after the literal text, we find a report on the transcript search, on exhibit search. May I take it that this is work products which should be taken out?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That should most certainly be taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, could I invite you to take that out and to destroy it immediately because it's there through mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Thank you very much for spotting that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned Slavo Krajisnik. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Slavo Krajisnik worked with Branko Ostojic and Sekovic down there, from the Birac region, and he worked in the company dealing with fuel. But I never saw him. We spoke over the phone twice and I don't think anything actually went through, went ahead. And I'm sure that he's not any relation of Mr. Krajisnik as far as Krajisnik is concerned. They're different areas. This was the Birac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we turn in the English to the third page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask: Are you aware of any oil or petrol trade that ever succeeded where Mr. Slavo Krajisnik was involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that there was anything like that. We went directly to the Jugopetrol company, as I see it says here, because the refinery price was better and there was no middleman to cater to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the same time you say it would be the price plus 3 dinars which is, from what I understand, the contribution to the party. So would that -- would you pay 3 dinars to Jugopetrol to be then transferred to the party or -- because you said "no middleman."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, had I -- no, I wouldn't have gone via Jugopetrol, it went via Raja Dukic's firm, and that would have calculated in the 3 dinars for the party. That would be the margin, the sales margin would be increased by 3 dinars only if we were to go through that company because the SDS had an agreement with that company for financial assistance. I wasn't in the Main Board at the time, so I can't know for sure what the arrangement was. And I don't think it would be relevant for you, anything that I would say in that regard because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any link between Slavo Krajisnik in his company and Mr. Dukic's company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think there is a link, not Dukic with Branko -- with Branko Ostojic, not Dukic. But I've actually forgotten, it was all a long time ago, you must understand. The business deal didn't go through, so I really can't remember. But there was some sort of story, whether with Ostojic or whoever, but I never met the man and I don't think it was anything terrible. Nothing secret. Everything went along these lines. Everything was legal and it was legal to set aside a portion for the party, for companies to set aside a portion for the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said you're not quite sure whether they were Slavo Krajisnik or Mirko Krajisnik, you explained to us that Slavo Krajisnik was not in any way related to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. That's at least how I understood it. When you referred to Mirko, were you referring to Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik's brother or -- you mentioned that name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I meant Mirko Krajisnik, Momcilo Krajisnik's brother. He worked in Rajko Dukic's company; that's not contested. And then there's this other man Krajisnik who has nothing to do, no relations. They are two companies, two individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, to turn, Mr. Bjelica, to the third page of this intercept, page 3 in the English as well. At the very bottom of the page we see reference to Mr. Dukic paying as well and Mr. Ostojic will pay as well. What is that a reference to, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, you can see here that those were two companies, one belonging to Ostojic, one Dukic's. And one Krajisnik worked with Dukic, another Krajisnik worked with Ostojic. In the Sokolac area, this activity was conducted by Milan Tupajic, and we decided to install a satellite antenna, a strong satellite antenna, reinforced, which could broadcast and catch programmes -- broadcast by state television from Serbia, from Yugoslavia, from Belgrade, because all the other transmitters were switched off by Radio Television Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we weren't -- we were in a complete media blockade. We had no programmes to watch. So we asked for offers from Belgrade, from the authorised company, and the offer was 26.000-odd convertible German marks for them to install and put into operation a system which would allow us to cover the Sokolac municipality and have a television signal -- radio and television signal coming from Belgrade, the Belgrade 2 programme, in fact. And in that conversation, I informed the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, Mr. Karadzic, of that because it is a -- the media blockade was a very major problem. We had information from Sarajevo, which was under the control of the Party of Democratic Action, and I said -- I told the president on that occasion that we had reinforced the Radio Romanija transmitter and that we were working with this new system, that we would do our best and via our sponsors and friends in the Serbian Democratic Party in Sokolac municipality, managed to collect 26.500 convertible German marks for that project. President Karadzic at the time asked us to look into the possibility of the technical feasibilities to reinforce the system so that it could be -- television programmes could be watched in Sarajevo as well. And I said in this conversation that we had no more resources and whether we could check this out. But he said that if need be, if we needed the resources and the funds, see if you could do it because it would be a good thing if the Serbs in Sarajevo should not only be able to watch Alija's television but Belgrade television programmes and all the rest. And then that difference, the additional money that should be paid to install a system of that kind, if possible, would be paid by Mr. Dukic and Mr. Ostojic. But as I say, this business transaction never went through because we didn't have the necessary resources. We had to build a repeater station and transmitter and that was all very expensive and we didn't have the money to do that. So I hope I have been able to explain what all this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turn back, please, to your 89(F) at tab 19, and I want to ask you about paragraph 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you learn about the ambush and killing of the people mentioned in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: As soon as something happened in the field, the signal centre would inform -- actually, the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade informed the signals centre, and then in their turn they would inform the families of the casualties, and those people from the signals centre were duty-bound to also inform the Municipal Assembly, and then the Municipal Assembly either would wait for somebody from the brigade command or on their own initiative inform or put somebody in charge of informing the families that an accident had happened and that people got killed. That's how I learnt of these people having been killed, that they had been ambushed. Bogdan Borovcanin, Darko Krsmanovic, Nenad Tabakovic, and this was very deep in the territory of the municipality of Sokolac. They were set fire to and their bodies were torched on the main road where there were no combat activities at all in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the paragraph immediately above that one, in other words, paragraph 14, you talked about "subversive and terrorist actions occurring." Why do you use those words?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: What else could you call this but terrorism if somebody plants explosives on the road or kill a person who is sowing their meadow or a shepherd in the field when you have a statement by the commander of the Patriotic League that they had obtained weapons and that he himself trained people in the area how to make explosives. 30 per cent at least, according to the list, were people who were engaged in the army and the police in the territory of Sokolac municipality and who were duty-bound to protect the territory of Sokolac on certain lines of separation and stay there. As they went there or as they were returning, they would be killed by explosives or hitting minefields. I'm sure that you have information that those were all booby-traps or anti-infantry mines that were planted on the road and that mostly these people either were killed or their lower extremities were injured, and I'm sure that you can find confirmation of that somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as paragraph 16 is concerned, could I invite you to look at that and then turn to tab 7 of the documents in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Tab 7? I saw a number 16 and now tab 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Paragraph 16 relates to tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So once you've read paragraph 16, turn to tab 7. Fortunately, all of these documents have been translated. Could I ask you: Where did you obtain the documents in tab 7 from?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Documents in tab 7 were obtained from the public security station in Sokolac or the security services centre in eastern Sarajevo in their department for documentation of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And shortly, if you can, explain to the Chamber why you obtained these documents.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, I've been following these trials to a certain extent and all the activities and investigations that have been conducted, and I see that only the Muslim and non-Serb victims are being mentioned in the territory of our municipalities. There were -- hadn't been no Serb casualties or if people had actually killed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And summarising these documents, we see that an investigation is carried out into the death of Mr. Krsmanovic. Could I ask you: What is his ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Krsmanovic, the late Krsmanovic, Sofren, was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the two people that I think were injured -- one was injured and one was unharmed, Rajko Eric and Milenko Krsmanovic, they were both Serbs as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And these documents detail the investigation into the death of one, the attack on the others. There are a number of names that the police suspect as perpetrators. We go to a document somewhere near the middle, dated the 20th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: On the same page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. Several pages on, please. Let me count how many for you, including the English. 13 pages on.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You'll see that the person that compiled this official report believed that the perpetrators may have been someone -- well, let me ask you to read the names. At the bottom of that page there are two names.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes. Izet Popara and Vahid Hajdarevic, who were Muslims and neighbours of the late Sofren and the late Eric and the others. The perpetrators' village was very nearby. They were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If one goes through this file and goes to the documents at the very end, one can see that as of the year 2000 no one has been brought to justice for these crimes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: That's right. Official reports were filed against unknown perpetrators; however, to this very day it hasn't been established who the perpetrators were. The case is still open for all crimes, not just for this crime; for everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, all those documents will be under D164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Do we have in the description of the documents we have, I think, a further specification of -- let me just check. Yes, we have a further specification. Mr. Josse, by the way, you asked the witness whether -- you say: One can see that as of the year 2000 -- no. Let me just -- let me just check what you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the year 2000 nobody by then was found guilty of these crimes -- of this crime, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, page 60, line 2 - and I more and more become aware of what a leading question is - invites the witness to confirm that the -- those who compiled the report were of the opinion that Mr. Hajdarevic and Popara might have been the perpetrators. At the same time, I see that this is an interview of Mr. Eric and it's not at all clear to me whether this opinion is the opinion of the -- of Mr. Cobovic and Vojinovic or whether it's the witness who is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As usual, and I mean this with the greatest respect, Your Honour is very beady eyed. It's my fault entirely. I would read it for what it's worth, that it's the opinion of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You ask a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I led the witness in the wrong way. I'm entirely at fault. I mean this in the full sense of the word, I'm entirely grateful to Your Honour for picking that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to follow the evidence as closely as possible, unless you would have reason that the witness could help us out that this is -- otherwise, we'll leave it at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't. And indeed to be fair to me, it wasn't that I particularly wanted to suggest that the police suspected these individuals as against a witness. I simply wanted to establish in fact that no one had ever been charged with these particular allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not that relevant. I'm not blaming you in any way of trying to achieve anything because it doesn't bring you that much, as a matter of fact, but apart from that, I insist, as always, on precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Might I observe, of course, that's what comes of asking leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, I -- my first line said, "I more and more become aware of what a leading question is."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you go back, Mr. Bjelica, to your 89(F) at tab 19, and could you look at paragraph 17. Only a few lines there. Just read them to yourself. And when you've done that, could you turn to tab 6, please. Again, you obtained these documents from your local police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And on this occasion, the victims of these crimes are Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to summarise the effect of this, they, it is alleged, had been murdered. And I don't suppose there's any dispute about that. If we go three pages from the back of tab 6 - so count three pages back, four in the English - we see the doctor's report where he verifies that all these unfortunate individuals were shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea whether the authorities were able to bring anyone to justice for these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I don't know what the court did and how far this has gone to. A file -- a report has been filed with the court. I don't know what the court has done so far. As far as I know, nobody has been tried, just like in the case of Krsmanovic and other cases. Everything is at a standstill, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could these documents have a number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, your --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. I'm trying to digest portions of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour 89(F) does not include, and I'm not criticising you for this, that was the Defence's decision any reference to the incident at Novoseoci. I may have pronounced that wrong. N-o-v-o-s-e-o-c-i. This was a massacre that occurred in the summer of 1992 in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Novoseoci.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. This was a massacre that occurred in the summer of 1992 in your municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: That's correct. I can see now that everything is correct and deserves every sort of condemnation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The victims, 44, were of Muslim ethnicity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What -- when did you learn of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: On one occasion, I don't know how long after that, Milan Tupajic told me on one occasion, he told me it seems to me these people from Novoseoci had a very unglorious ending. He told me something to that effect. Don't hold me on to that. I don't know what words he used, how he interpreted the event. I know that nobody spoke about the event. At that time or before that time, the army spoke about disarming the villages, that the whole area of Romanija is at risk because of these units that were moving about. Maybe I can say something more about that later. But when I learnt -- I didn't know how many people were involved, how many were executed. In my view, this was unnecessary. On one occasion, I believe that this was a few years after the event, there was a religious holiday of some sort, All Saints' Day, or St. Mark's Day or some anniversary. In any case, a day when you go to the cemeteries, and I met -- I bumped into the father of a lad who had committed suicide, and I asked him about another person whose name I can mention. And this man says: Well, I'm trying to get by. This was a great misfortune, and see what Krstic had done; he took these children, he took them to Novoseoci. I never knew that this guy had been there, and there was him and two other lads, and then he says he was persecuted by that all the time, he couldn't sleep, and before the eyes of his parents he had committed suicide. And this was more or less what I learnt from the parents of one of the lads, and he also mentioned another lad who were together -- who was together with him and participated in the -- in the incident. I finally learned the number when the place had been identified and when the victims had been discovered, when their remains had been discovered, and the post mortem had been carried out, then I became absolutely aware of what had happened. And for a while there were rumours, the village was rife with rumours about these people, that they were actually away on work obligation, that they would be exchanged, and only later did it turn out that it was all not true. And I don't think that any other bodies knew of that, not even the president of the municipality Mr. Pajic, who was also president of the Crisis Staff, knew about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So not to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the witness mentioned -- said that someone told him: Well, I'm trying to get by. This was a great misfortune, and see what Krstic had done. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was exactly what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, you went to a funeral some years later. When was the funeral, the funeral where you received this information? Which year, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I can't remember. I believe that it was at the end of the war, towards the end of the war. And it was not a funeral. This guy had already been buried, a monument had been erected. I came across his father, whom I knew very well. And I knew that his son had committed suicide. I don't know why, I don't know what the motives of the suicide were. I don't know what the family had to go through and what problems they were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My fault. And the father told you something about Krstic. Can you be more precise as to what he said about --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: This is what he told me. He accused Krstic of the death of his child. He says: See what Krstic did to us. He dragged our children into all that, and I said: What that? And he said: All that thing that happened around Novoseoci. And as a result of that, his late son had nightmares, problems, and then finally, right before the eyes of his parents, he did what he did. This is all what he told me, what I knew, what I learnt about the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you understand him to be saying about Krstic? What was he suggesting that Krstic had, in fact, done -- or alluding to rather than suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Probably, but not only probably but certainly, it was Krstic who had issued the order to do whatever was done. I can't see anything else as a possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Your Honour, unless the Bench has any questions on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was a -- the name "Krstic" is not unique.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, it's General Krstic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The man who was convicted of the Srebrenica massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're talking about the same person, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next matter I'd like to ask you about - again a completely different topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know whether this would be a convenient moment, Your Honour, moving on to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you've moving to another subject, this would be a convenient moment. We'll have another break, Mr. Bjelica, until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The topic I now want you to tell the Chamber something about is the visit of, among others, Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik to Sokolac on the 17th of May of 1992. It's not in your 89(F), Mr. Bjelica. Again, a decision of the Defence that we wanted you to tell the Court orally about that particular occasion. Let me guide you a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had some guests coming from Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: These were not guests -- actually, they were guests, but those were people who hailed from Sokolac who resided in Belgrade, mostly executives, doctors who hailed from the area and they wanted to come and visit the area where they originated from because we can say that at the time Sokolac was completely encircled by the enemy, that the entire region of Romanija was at a risk of a huge material disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm going to lead on this, and I'll be stopped if my learned friends have any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because this does deal with issues evidently -- specifically directed to the accused, it would be better in this area if Mr. Josse didn't lead. We will be sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm being -- I'm only interrupting because I'm not going to lead on Mr. Krajisnik. I'm simply dealing with the guests who were coming from Belgrade at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the warning is there, and Mr. Margetts also knows that although he's sensitive on the matter, the Chamber invites him certainly not to be oversensitive. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I simply wanted to deal with how these guests were going to get there from Belgrade. And it's right, isn't it, that there was a military hospital in Sokolac. People were -- wounded were being ferried by helicopter from that hospital to Belgrade, and it was decided that some of the returnees from Belgrade could take a helicopter ride back, so to speak, from Belgrade to Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: It is correct that was there a military hospital in Sokolac. Those who were more heavily wounded were referred to the military medical academy in Belgrade. There were lots of wounded every day. Every day a helicopter would transport the wounded and would come back empty from Belgrade. Those who wanted to come to Sokolac, some of them doctors, some of them executives -- and the road was not safe. There was a road block near Visegrad. You couldn't get to Rogatica because in Gorazde from Medjedja to Foca the roads were also blocked, and in order for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm stopping you, Mr. Bjelica. That is why I wanted to lead. It is not in dispute, I'm sure. That's how these people got there from Belgrade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: By helicopter, because it wasn't safe to travel by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: They had to take the helicopter because there was a risk at every step of the way that they would be targeted by the Muslim terrorists if they had decided to take any of the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did you - when I say "you," the municipal authorities - also invite various members of the leadership of the Republika Srpska to attend on the same occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: We organised a meeting of executives from Sokolac and those who had arrived from Belgrade. We could not convey the situation in the general region of Republika Srpska to our friends, and in order to have them fully informed about the political and economic situation, we asked the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic; the president of the National Assembly; somebody from the government; a few ministers; vice-president of Republika Srpska, and the newly appointed commander of the Main Staff and his associates, to come and to talk to our guests and to inform them about the situation, whether the situation was good or not, whether it was safe when -- how these people could be involved into sending humanitarian aid to their own people because they knew that we were in dire straits and Muslim saboteurs had destroyed our transmission lines, our main transmission lines that served to feed Romanija with electricity. We had been without electricity for six months, which we needed for the wounded, for the injured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you very clearly explained why you invited the leadership of the Republika Srpska, and then you continued to explain that by demonstrating how awful your situation was and who was to be blamed for that. I'm not saying that it's not right or -- what you say, but it was not a portion of the question. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So we -- you've told us that, among others, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik attended. What --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- were they shown? Where were they taken? Mr. Krajisnik in particular I'm asking about. What happened on the day, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: They were not taken anywhere. Nothing was shown to them. They arrived in the meeting hall of the Sokolac municipality straight from Pale and they returned to Pale. They did not even have time to have lunch. And the rest of us stayed, having lunch with our friends from Belgrade and other members of the delegation. Those people were in a hurry and I don't know whether something had happened or some international representatives were supposed to come for a meeting. I know that they didn't even stay for lunch, that immediately after the meeting they headed for Pale and the rest of us stayed at lunch. In other words, their stay boiled down to them sitting down in the meeting hall of the Municipal Assembly building in Sokolac, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you can be precise, but only if you can be precise, could you tell the Chamber what dealings you had with Mr. Krajisnik that day.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I didn't have any direct contacts with him because that meeting was not planned like that. There were no individual contacts. The leadership came, the president of the republic, the president of the National Assembly, and somebody from the government - I don't know who - some of the vice-presidents, I can't remember who he was. They came, they sat down in the meeting room, and there were no individual contacts between them or -- and anybody else. There's some 70 people sitting there, some former politicians from the former system, some retired officers, some executives. There were no individual contacts. This was just not planned. When they started to leave, they may have been stopped by a journalist, but that was all. That is all the contacts that leadership had with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to ask you about. The contact with a journalist, one or more journalists, did you listen to Mr. Krajisnik or Dr. Karadzic's conversation or conversations with those journalists?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, one or two clarifying questions. Did any of the persons you mentioned, did they address the meeting? Did they speak to the 70 persons being present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned the president of the republic. Did he address the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned the president of the Assembly. Did he address the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they all said something. It was primarily the president of the republic and the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, who were primarily asked to address the audience. Then Mr. Krajisnik took the floor, he made a contribution, and some other people also asked to take the floor. However, President Karadzic and General Mladic had the main say at the meeting; they were the keynote speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were the journalist present during these addresses made by the three persons you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. Nothing was hidden. And there were not just three persons. Maybe 10 or 15 people spoke but there were two keynote speakers who were in charge of informing the gathering of whatever was necessary. That was the president of the republic and the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic. Could you turn to tab 12, please. This is another collection of documents that you have provided to the Defence. That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this details military prosecutions - correct me if I'm wrong about that - or prosecutions of members of the VRS for various alleged crimes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Which one? Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: There was a crime involved. Serbs wanted to take something from a Serb, and those things were processed. Whenever a report was filed, these things ended up in court. There was no anarchy. The police did their job within the boundaries of their capabilities under such circumstances. This is just to support the thesis that there was no anarchy, unlike some people said that everybody did what they wanted to do. Those who were involved in crimes were brought in regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, in fact, as you've, I think, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we need a number for this first, or for this bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I think you just explained, you've said Serbs wanted to take something from Serbs, so in all of these cases the alleged perpetrators of the crimes are Serbian and the alleged victims are also of Serb ethnicity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, one question also to clarify. You said: "Irrespective of their ethnicity, those who were involved in crimes were brought in." At that time, the -- how many Muslims were left in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. In the town of Sokolac there were not many Muslims even before the war. The municipality had some 15.000 inhabitants and 4.000 of them were Muslims. In the town itself, there may have been a few dozens of households -- Muslim households, and some of them exchanged property with the Serbs from other areas in -- even before the war, so there were not that many Muslims in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said 4.000 in the municipality. How many of them were left, or how many families, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, towards the end of 1992, or in the second half of 1992, I can't remember exactly, very few of them left. In 1990 through the villages, Vrbare, Buta [phoen], or maybe some other villages that were there, and they stayed there until 1993 or 1994. The others had left after the agreement in Knezevo now with the president of the municipality of Olovo, Mr. Dzeved Abazovic, and the negotiations were led by Milan Tupajic, the president of the municipality of Sokolac, and since they thought at the time the war would not last long, and that's why they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand there were a few dozens of households in the town, whereas you have no information on the remainder of the municipality and how many still were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very few. Very few. Maybe 30 or 40 families altogether at the most. Very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's one document in tab 12 that we would invite you to particularly look at. It's, unfortunately, very near the middle. It's dated the 18th of November of 1992, and it's a report on recognition of a person, and it's an alleged attempted murder filed by someone called Cedo Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I -- it's my fault, Mr. Bjelica. I'm going to, in fact, ask you not to look at that for a moment. I want to return to the questions that the learned Judge has just asked. He asked you -- this is the learned Presiding Judge asked you, that there were a few dozen households in the town, whereas you have no information on the remainder of the municipality, how many were still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, Mr. Josse, that I said no precise information but that has not appeared in the transcript, but I stand corrected if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is what I heard as well, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there's any need, we could listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And your answer was: "Very few, very few." When you used the --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: A few dozen of houses or households, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you used the words "very few," what were you referring to; the town or the municipality as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The municipality as a whole. If there had been 4.000 Muslims before the war, only a few hundred remained, which is very few in comparison with the number that had lived there before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next want you to turn, please, to tab 15. There are two documents there. They are, unfortunately, untranslated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question before we go to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D166, Mr. Josse, is about the theft of a blue Lada 1600. You initially asked the witness to move to another portion of that material. Then you said: No, please do not. Does that mean that not the whole of D166 is material which you would like to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, that doesn't mean that. We would like to tender it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There was a specific point that I was going to draw the witness's attention to, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- on instructions, there is no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before these are given a number, the Chamber, I dare say, would like to know where you have obtained these documents from, and then you can explain what they are. So first question is: Where have you obtained these two documents from?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Mostly in the municipality or municipality committees of veterans' organisations in the territory of the municipality, if they dealt with veterans, and in the municipalities and in the hospitals where the wounded were hospitalised. They are from various institutions, from the hospital, from the municipality, or veterans' organisations. And all these documents have been filed with respective records, and there are even some death certificates there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you read the title of the first document.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: "People who were either injured or killed in the territory of Sokolac municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it is right, isn't it, that looking at number 1, it talks a Dragicevic Rade being killed in an ambush on October the 20th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, Rade Dragicevic, yes, at the Beta mountain on the territory of Sokolac municipality, the father of four children. He was gathering firewood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Number 2 is Ilija Macar, who was killed when stepping on a land-mine?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Ilija Macar and his wife, Slobodanka Macar Ceranic. They were on their way from a funeral, the funeral of her brother-in-law and on their way to the village, they stepped on a land-mine and both of them were heavily injured and succumbed to their wounds on the way to the hospital. Husband and wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Kezunovic Lazo, number 3, was also killed in an ambush?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Lazo Kezunovic and Maksim Vukovic were killed in an ambush, and they were torched. And nothing remained but a few body parts and ashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the ambush in which they were killed? Do you know any details about it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I don't know anything. It was not just the two of them who were killed. Some 20 cars or so came by and there must have been 30 or so casualties. There is information on that. I took just the information about two people from Sokolac. There were other people, from Rogatica, for example, Viljko Bojevic and his brother, a director of a company, they were on their way to purchase some supplies. So the two brothers Bojkovic were killed, and I have to apologise to all the other victims of that event for having taken just the data on these two people from Sokolac. This happened on the main road between Sokolac and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The second document details individuals who were killed on or near their property?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- it was unclear to us from the witness's last answer exactly what these documents purport to be. It appeared that the witness referred to sources of information but not exactly to how these specific documents were compiled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Mr. Josse, you asked where he obtained them, but how they were compiled is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially the last answer of the witness raises some questions in this respect. Could you please explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, did you produce this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: I just systematised this. They were all documents and records in the police station about this and they were never brought in, just like -- or rather, they were never finalised. All the criminal reports were filed against perpetrators unknown. All this was in the police station in Sokolac, Rogatica, Zvornik, each of these names and surnames. And I say that with full responsibility, that in the public security station, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Rogatica and Vogosca, everything belonging to the security services of Zvornik, all these names are to be found in those police stations. And I think that the office for tracing missing persons and Office for Cooperation with the Tribunal have handed these documents over to the Prosecution, to the OTP, or wherever, and that they have been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to move on, Your Honour. I'm in the Court's hands as to whether they should be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you want to tender them -- I mean, of course the whole -- I would say all of the information is in the witness's testimony to the extent -- to the other extent, we can't read it at this moment. You would need a translation. And from what I understand, the purpose of these documents is to present to the Chamber at least these four examples of how people in Sokolac died; as a result of ambushes or mines laid by whomever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I don't think there's any need to give it a number. Please proceed. But I leave it to you, if you insist to have it -- but then you need to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's being translated again. We could try and have it withdrawn, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't insist on giving it a number. Then let's refrain from doing it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turn briefly, if we could, to tab 14. Who compiled this list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: This list was compiled by the board of the families of dead fighters and missing persons, persons detained and missing from the Pale municipality. Then the president of that board was Mr. Cicovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And could you read the title of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: "List of fallen fighters --" because they are listed as fighters, they were members of the army -- "from Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And after that, can you turn to the next list. That is a list of servicemen who were injured in the course of the conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: This was not a conflict. The data about the wounded persons come from the military hospital in Sokolac where they were taken and given medical assistance, and it was agreed between the command in Zepa and the army that the unit should go to Zlovrh, where the repeater stations are, to replace the young soldiers there and to leave food and fuel for the repeater stations. They did not expect to encounter any problems. The unit set out, and when they went through a canyon, they weren't ready for any fighting. They had no intention in engaging in any battles or fighting. The extremists from Zepa, from various weapons and artillery pieces, opened fire, and that's what happened. On the one hand they say they had nothing, that they weren't armed, whereas the unit that set out in a humanitarian -- on a humanitarian assignment, we can call it that, this is what they experienced and what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, again, is this again related to Zepa or -- because that seems to appear from the answer of the witness. Could perhaps the witness read the title just above the second document. Could you please read that, Mr. Bjelica, so just the handwritten title. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes. "List of injured and wounded fighters, Zepa, 1992." I got this from the military hospital in Sokolac, the 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4th of June. What -- it's for the first time that we now get information about Zepa, Mr. Josse. Is there any specific link to Sokolac or -- I mean -- or is it just that you say: I would like to give a broad view on what happened in that part of the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why have you obtained this information is the question I'd like to ask, Mr. Bjelica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, there were fighters, people from Sokolac there, and this happened on the border between the Sokolac and Rogatica-Han Pijesak municipalities. And the participants were people from Sokolac; that's why I'm talking about it. And that's the border of the two municipalities, and it's directly linked to Sokolac. It's the same brigade. Now, whether they were from Pale, more from Pale or more from Sokolac, in any particular unit, that is debatable, and it's not essential here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It also introduces a new element, Mr. Josse, because although the witness seems on grounds not immediately clear to me, sources not immediately clear, that we now entered into the area of listing in some detail the casualties among combatants, which is, as far as I am aware of, not the core of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask for a number for these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst dealing with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't finish my last thing when I said because although the witness seems on grounds not immediately clear to me, sources not immediately clear, I should have continued and said more or less denies or at least puts in question whether there were combatants, being soldiers, not having arms, et cetera. I'm not inviting you to explore the matter, but I read on the transcript, which happens to me now and then, that I start a part of a sentence and do not finish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to lead the witness on a portion of his evidence which has been notified to my learned friend. He'll stop me if he's unhappy with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He'll ask us to stop you, Mr. Josse, perhaps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right that you have some knowledge of an attack by Muslim forces in a place called Jabucko Sedlo on August the 20th, 1992? Is the answer to that yes, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right that, as you understand it, there was a delivery of humanitarian assistance to the Serbian community in Gorazde, which was taking place --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and five men were ambushed and killed. And you can provide their names if asked. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where does your information of that particular attack come from?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: The same as everything else; the military hospital in Sokolac informed the leadership of the municipality about people from the municipality, so we had to see to the families and the population. And nobody wanted to do this kind of work so they would transfer this duty to the municipality, tell the family that their member has been killed or wounded. So this was unpleasant, an unpleasant duty that we had to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How do you know that it was a humanitarian convoy these people were involved with?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA
utterances.text: Well, certainly it was because in Gorazde, at Jabucko, the Serbs were in a very difficult situation and they needed assistance. On the one hand they were cut off, they couldn't go to Rogatica, or -- that would be the safest route otherwise, and the decision was taken by the unit that they should provide -- well, there were civilian vehicles from the Romanija-Sokolac firm that were being used and they were driving food, taking food, whereas security was provided by soldiers, some of the army. And I don't know what the name of the place was now, but it was between Mesici and Jabuka -- Jabucko Sedlo, actually. They were stopped there -- or rather, came across an ambush, and they were looted. Five or six persons were killed including Curovic Predrag, Bjelakovic Radisa, Vidovic Radomir, Srdjan Djeric, Jovanovic Ilija. Their remains were never found. And later on we learnt that they were caught alive, captured alive and liquidated in Gorazde and thrown into the Drina River, but their bodies were never found, their bodily remains were never found, so that they are listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I am looking at the clock and wonder how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My firm intention is to use one more session and one more session only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please finish this part and then we'll consider --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have finished. Then we'll first invite Mr. Bjelica not to follow the usher, as usual, but, Mr. Bjelica, we will continue tomorrow. Most likely we'll have a later start, Mr. Josse, because there's a swearing in ceremony of new Judges and I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would have an opportunity -- let's first ask Mr. Bjelica to be escorted out of the courtroom. Mr. Bjelica, we'll start tomorrow, most likely anything between quarter past 9.00, 9.30, approximately, in this same courtroom. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or the testimony you are still about to give tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could then the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. Could you -- would you please follow the security officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Shall I leave this here?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The documents, please, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, of course I'm asking -- I did ask you because we -- I wondered whether we could finish the witness by tomorrow. Mr. Margetts, do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just add this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. He is as keen as every witness to get back to his home country as soon as possible. He tells me he has a Status Conference in his case on the 14th of April. The sooner he is back, the sooner he can prepare with his lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Mr. Margetts, much of the evidence led by the Defence is of a character which I can imagine that there's not -- I don't know exactly what the position of the Prosecution is, but we often heard that some attacks, some ambushes, some crimes committed by unknown perpetrators, and therefore not prosecuted nor -- well, no follow-up, it's -- I asked Mr. Josse in the very beginning on what we had to focus on, whether it would undermine the -- or contest the evidence led by the Prosecution. He said it was mainly that rather than, although perhaps also, about sentencing. I wonder whether we should go in every detail -- I mean, whether there was a Lada 1600 and whether it was blue or not. I mean, I don't know what the position of the Prosecution is, but the Chamber might be a bit reluctant to go into every single detail of what certainly are crimes reported, sometimes with a follow-up, sometimes without a follow-up, sometimes rather unclear, such as people being killed by mines. I don't know whether we have to go in every detail of who laid mines in what area of this municipality. So I wonder whether, keeping this in mind, whether we could finish tomorrow. I was already informed by Mr. Registrar that if we could have a late start, we could have a late finish as well. So we would not lose that time but we would have our full time available. That would be two sessions for the Prosecution. Would that do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously we're always reluctant to make time commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know you're reluctant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But in this circumstance with Your Honour's comments, I think shared by us as well, so we expect we would be able to finish in two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then of course there might be a lot of questions by the Judges, we'll see. But we have at least an opportunity to continue beyond a quarter to 2.00 and therefore have the full time available. Nevertheless, I'd like to start tomorrow morning as soon as possible. So if everyone -- officially the swearing in ceremony has been scheduled for half an hour, but if we would be ready by quarter past 9.00 it would be highly appreciated if we could then immediately start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll mention to your legal officer when Your Honour has risen one subsequent or consequential scheduling difficulty there might be of sitting too late into tomorrow afternoon. I can do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not too late, as a matter of fact. We have limited time because there will be a Status Conference in the afternoon, but it will not start at a quarter past 2.00, as usual the afternoon sessions do start. So I'm not thinking about more than compensating for the half an hour. If you need another 15 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have a brief word, of course in the presence of my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, same courtroom, quarter past 9.00 up till 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of April, 2006, at 9.15 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
